title: Glossary of Terms of the Sutra of the Primal Vows of the Earth-Store Bodhisattva
author: Compiled by Mingde
excerpt: Things to Know When Reciting the Sutra of the Primal Vows of the Earth-Store Bodhisattva

inline.s: The Sutra of the Primal Vows of the Earth-Store Bodhisattva
Compiled by Mingde

blocks.text: Chapter One: The Spiritual Penetrations of the Palace of Trayastrimsa

inline.s: The Buddha spoke the Dharma in the Trayastrimsa heaven for the sake of his mother; the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions gathered together in praise; the Tathagata smiled and emitted clouds of light, and brought forth subtle sounds; the gods, dragons, ghosts, and spirits of the ten directions also all gathered; and the Buddha told the bodhisattva Manjusri of the Earth-Store Bodhisattva’s past causal grounds.

[The Earth-Store Bodhisattva] Because this bodhisattva “abides unmoved, patient as the great earth, and contemplates in deep stillness, hidden as a secret treasure,” he is therefore named Earth-Store. After the World-Honored One’s nirvāṇa and before Maitreya’s descent, the Earth-Store Bodhisattva bears the heavy responsibility of saving the sentient beings of the Sahā world in which we dwell, and he dwells constantly in the hells to remove their suffering, having the vow “until the hells are empty, I will not become a Buddha”; therefore he is renowned for his “great vow.” Sincerely reciting “Namo the Great-Vowed Ksitigarbha King Bodhisattva” dispels calamities and difficulties, and the merit is immeasurable.
[Original vow] The fundamental vow made by a bodhisattva when he first resolves his mind.

[Trayastrimsa] The name of a heaven; the character “dao...” is pronounced “dāo.” The heavens number twenty-eight layers in all; Trayastrimsa is the second layer, and its lord is Shakra. One day and night in this heaven equals a hundred years in the human world.
[Palace] The palace in which the lord of the heaven dwells.

[Spiritual power] That which is unfathomable in its transformations is called “spirit,” and that which freely penetrates without obstruction is called “power.” This is the wondrous function that issues forth from one’s own nature: the divine eye, divine ear, knowledge of others’ minds, knowledge of past lives, the power of psychic travel, and the power of the extinction of the outflows — six in all.

[The power of the extinction of the outflows] An abbreviation of the power of the wisdom of the extinction of the outflows. “Outflows” are a name for afflictions; “extinction of the outflows” means cutting off all afflictions completely.
[Chapter] Equivalent to “section.” For example, “Chapter One: The Spiritual Penetrations of the Palace of Trayastrimsa” means “Chapter One, the Spiritual Penetrations of the Palace of Trayastrimsa.”
[Thus have I heard] “I personally heard the Buddha say thus.” “I” refers to Ānanda, the Buddha’s cousin and attendant; this sutra was recited by him when the scriptures were compiled.
[At one time] At that time. Here it refers to the time when the Buddha spoke the Dharma, that is, when teacher and student were in accord, when the capacity and the teaching responded to each other.
[The Buddha] Refers to Śākyamuni Buddha.

[His mother] Refers to Śākyamuni Buddha’s mother, Lady Maya. The Buddha manifested as a prince of the Kapilavastu kingdom in India, named Siddhartha; seven days after his birth, his mother left the human world and ascended to the Trayastrimsa heaven. Before his nirvāṇa the Buddha went to the Trayastrimsa heaven for three things: first, to speak the Dharma for his mother and repay his mother’s kindness; second, to bid farewell and console the heavenly host; third, to entrust the Earth-Store Bodhisattva with a charge.

[The ten directions] Refers to east, south, west, north (the four directions), southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest (the four corners), and above and below. Extending out in these ten directions there are immeasurable, boundless worlds.
[Inconceivable] That which ordinary language, words, and thought cannot reach is called “inconceivable.”
[Bodhisattva] An abbreviation of the Sanskrit “bodhisattva”; rendered into Chinese as “enlightened being,” that is, a sentient being who can both enlighten himself and enlighten others.

[Mahasattva] An abbreviation of “mahasattva”; the character “he” is pronounced “hē.” Rendered into Chinese as “great mind” or “great sentient being,” it refers to a sentient being having the great mind to become a Buddha, that is, a great bodhisattva.

[Sentient beings] “Sentient beings” are those born from the union of many conditions, and the term includes insentient beings (referring to such things as mountains, rivers, the great earth, and plants, which have no conscious activity) and sentient beings. The Dharma-Drum Sutra says: “The ten thousand dharmas combined and set up are called sentient beings.” But the term “sentient beings” in the scriptures and treatises usually refers to conscious living beings, that is, all living animals that have consciousness, and so it is also called “living beings.”

[The five turbidities] First, the turbidity of the kalpa, meaning the age encounters misfortune and calamities arise frequently; second, the turbidity of afflictions, meaning the minds of the people of the world are filled with greed, anger, and delusion; third, the turbidity of sentient beings, meaning sentient beings are of low capacity, with much suffering and little joy; fourth, the turbidity of views, meaning false views prevail and thought is confused; fifth, the turbidity of life, meaning sentient beings, recompensed by evil karma, are worn out in body and mind and have short lives.
[Evil world] A world in which evil deeds flourish.
[Obstinate and hard] Because of heavy afflictions one cannot hear the truth and does not accept the teaching of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
[Knowing the Dharma of suffering and joy] Truly knowing what is suffering and what is joy, and how to leave suffering and attain joy.

[World-Honored One] An honorific title for Śākyamuni Buddha. The Buddha is most honored and most venerable in the world and beyond the world, alone exalted among the nine dharma-realms (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas).

[The world and beyond the world] The world and the world-transcending. “The world” is the world of ordinary beings in the six paths; “beyond the world” is the world of arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The former is called the six ordinary paths, or the six destinies; the latter is called the four noble paths.
[The six paths] Hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods.
[At that time] The time when the Buddhas had sent their attendants to ask after the Buddha’s well-being.
[Tathagata] One of the ten titles of the Buddha; here it refers to Śākyamuni Buddha.
[Cloud] A metaphor for the light being as abundant as colored clouds.
[The great Prajñā-luster cloud] Prajñā, rendered into Chinese, is “wisdom.” “Prajñā” is pronounced “bō rě.”
[The great Samādhi-luster cloud] “Samādhi” is also called “samma” (samadhana), rendered into Chinese as “concentration.”
[The great refuge-luster cloud] “Refuge” means to return and to rely upon.
[Paramita] Rendered into Chinese as “reaching the other shore.” Crossing from this shore of birth and death, through the middle current of afflictions, to the other shore of nirvāṇa.

[Nirvāṇa] Rendered into Chinese as “perfect stillness”; perfect means perfect in all the virtues of wisdom, stillness means stilling all the afflictions and karma. Also translated as “extinction and transcendence”; extinction means extinguishing the afflictions of views and thought, the afflictions of dust and sand, and the affliction of ignorance; transcendence means passing beyond the birth and death of the divided portion and the birth and death of transformation. This is the real thusness realm attained by the noble ones, neither arising nor ceasing, transcending time and space; and it is also the most ideal and most beautiful final home of the countless beings.
[The birth and death of the divided portion] The birth and death of the divided portion is the physical birth and death that ordinary beings undergo within the three realms.

[The birth and death of transformation] Refers to the mental birth and death of thought that arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and great bodhisattvas — who have already gone beyond the round of the three realms — experience beyond the three realms.

[The three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world of sentient beings possessing the two desires of sex and food: the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, up to the heaven of the enjoyment of others’ transformations in the heaven-realm, all belong to the realm of desire; the realm of form is the world of sentient beings without the two desires of sex and food but still possessing form (in Buddhist learning “form” refers to all material things that have shape and occupy space), from the Brahma hosts heaven up to Mahesvara heaven, all belonging to the realm of form; and above Mahesvara heaven, up to the heaven of neither thinking nor not-thinking, all belong to the formless realm, the world of sentient beings who, lacking the two desires of sex and food and form alike, abide their mind-consciousness in deep marvelous concentration. These three realms are all realms in which ordinary beings go and come through birth and death.

[The six perfections] Also named the six paramitas; these are the great practices of the bodhisattva, by which one can cross from this shore of birth and death to the other shore of nirvāṇa. Their content has six: first, giving; second, keeping the precepts; third, patience; fourth, diligence; fifth, concentration; sixth, prajñā.

[Prajñā] Rendered into Chinese as wisdom, but this wisdom is the Tathagata’s complete and constant great awakening. In the scriptures and treatises, to distinguish it from the clever wisdom of ordinary worldly people, the transliteration “prajñā” is always used.
[Dana-paramita] That is, the perfection of giving.
[Sila-paramita] That is, the perfection of keeping the precepts.
[Ksanti-paramita] That is, the perfection of patience. The character “chan” is pronounced “chàn.”
[Virya-paramita] That is, the perfection of diligence. The character “pi” is pronounced “pí.”
[Dhyana-paramita] That is, the perfection of concentration.
[Prajñā-paramita] That is, the perfection of wisdom.

[The sound of kindness and compassion, the sound of joy and equanimity] Kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity are the “four immeasurable minds”: the immeasurable mind of kindness, the immeasurable mind of compassion, the immeasurable mind of joy, and the immeasurable mind of equanimity. Giving joy to all sentient beings is called the “immeasurable mind of kindness”; removing the suffering of all sentient beings is called the “immeasurable mind of compassion”; seeing others practice good or be freed from suffering and attain joy, and being deeply joyful, is called the “immeasurable mind of joy”; and as for the above three minds, letting them go without clinging, treating enemy and kin equally, without giving rise to love or hate, is called the “immeasurable mind of equanimity.”

[The sound of liberation] Sentient beings are tightly bound by the three poisons (greed, anger, and delusion); studying the Buddha-dharma they can attain liberation. The World-Honored One, wishing to cause sentient beings to be forever free of the three poisons and ultimately peaceful, brought forth the sound of liberation.
[The sound of the outflows] “Outflows” are a name for afflictions. “Without outflows” means pure and free of afflictions.
[The sound of wisdom] Hearing this sound increases wisdom. The “wisdom” here refers to the common prajñā.
[The sound of great wisdom] The “wisdom” here refers to the uncommon prajñā.

[The common prajñā and the uncommon prajñā] When the Buddha speaks the Prajñā sutra, it is divided into the common and the uncommon kinds. That which is common to the dharmas of the sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas is called the common prajñā; that which speaks only of the dharmas practiced by the bodhisattvas, that is, not common to the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, is called the uncommon prajñā.

[The lion’s roar, the great lion’s roar] “Lion” refers to the lion. A metaphor that the Buddha speaks the Dharma like the lion’s roar, with a mind without fear, able to subdue the false teachings of the heterodox. “The lion’s roar” is a metaphor for speaking the Dharma of the three vehicles (the sravaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle); “the great lion’s roar” is a metaphor for speaking the Dharma of the great vehicle.

[Sahā] An abbreviation of the name of the Sahā world in which we dwell. “Sahā” is rendered into Chinese as “enduring.” Because the sentient beings of this world are able to endure the ten evils (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, idle speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, anger, and delusion) and all afflictions without being willing to leave, it is called “the world of endurance.”

[Heavenly dragons] That is, the “eight classes of heavenly beings and dragons.” The heavens and the dragons are two, and the foremost, of the eight classes. The eight classes: heavens, dragons, yakshas, gandharvas, asuras, garudas, kinnaras, mahoragas.

[The six paths] Heavens, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, hells. Because these six are the places to which all sentient beings go according to their karma, they are also called the “six destinies.”
[Karma] All our good and evil thoughts and actions are called karma; for example, good thoughts and good actions are called “good karma,” and bad thoughts and bad actions are called “evil karma.”

[Asura] Rendered into Chinese as “not a god” and “without virtue,” because the sentient beings of this path, in their spiritual powers and merit, surpass the human path and are much like the gods; only that, when they were in their causal stage, though they cultivated merit, they still carried minds of anger and pride, and so they have the blessed fortune of gods but not the virtue of gods.

[Heavens] The heavenly path has twenty-eight heavens in all; the first is the heaven of the four great kings, the second is Trayastrimsa, and the highest is the heaven of neither thinking nor not-thinking.

[The heaven of the four great kings] The heavenly realm in which the four great kings dwell (the eastern king who upholds the kingdom, the southern king who increases, the western king of wide eyes, and the northern king of much learning).

[Tusita heaven] That is, the Tusita heaven. “Tusita” is pronounced “Tusita,” rendered into Chinese as “contentment”; the heavenly beings here have few desires and are content. The inner court is where the bodhisattva of one lifetime to Buddhahood (this bodhisattva needs only this one lifetime to fill the Buddha’s place) resides; the future-descending bodhisattva Maitreya currently dwells here; the outer court is the dwelling of the ordinary heavenly beings. One day and night in this heaven equals four hundred years in the human world.
[Brahma] Pronounced “fàn.” Brahma means pure.
[Mahesvara heaven] Rendered into Chinese as “the heaven of great freedom”; the character “xi” is pronounced “xī.”

[The heaven of neither thinking nor not-thinking] The concentration of the heavenly beings of this heaven has no gross thought, and is called “no thought”; and still has subtle thought, and is called “not no-thought.”
[The heavenly host] The many heavenly beings.
[The dragon host] The many dragon-spirits.
[Ghosts and spirits] Sentient beings of the ghost path; those with merit are called “spirits,” and those without merit are called “ghosts.”
[Devour] The character “dan” is pronounced “dàn”; the same as “dan” (to eat or be eaten).
[The ghost-king of evil eyes, the ghost-king who devours blood, the ghost-king who devours vital essence, the ghost-king who devours embryos and eggs, the ghost-king who spreads disease]
These five belong to the evil ghost-kings.

[The poison-absorbing ghost-king, the kind-hearted ghost-king, the beneficent ghost-king, the greatly reverent ghost-king] These four are good ghost-kings, always making the benefit of sentient beings their refuge.
[The poison-absorbing ghost-king] He absorbs the poisons of the ten thousand things and does not harm sentient beings.
[The kind-hearted ghost-king] He loves and thinks of sentient beings and removes all fear.
[The beneficent ghost-king] He has merit, and helps people accomplish good dharmas.

[The greatly reverent ghost-king] He belongs to the good spirits that protect the Dharma. He and his retinue (“retinue” means his underlings) protect with mindfulness those who uphold the three refuges, the five precepts, and the bodhisattva precepts in accordance with the Dharma.
[The bodhisattva Manjusri] That is, the bodhisattva Manjusri; among all the bodhisattvas he is first in wisdom.

[Prince of the Dharma] An honorific title for the great bodhisattvas. The Buddha is king of the Dharma; the bodhisattvas are the successors to the Buddha’s place, and so the bodhisattvas are called princes of the Dharma.

[To address respectfully] One below addressing one above is called “bai” (to report); one above addressing one below is called “gao” (to announce). When both mutually respect each other it is also called “bai.”
[Even with my Buddha-eye, I cannot fully count it] A grand statement of the exceeding number of sentient beings that the Earth-Store Bodhisattva has saved, layer upon layer without end.

[All these are sentient beings whom the Earth-Store Bodhisattva, from kalpas long ago, has already saved, is to save, has not yet saved; already accomplished, is to accomplish, has not yet accomplished.] Among the countless great hosts gathered here, “already saved, already accomplished” refers to those who have already become Buddhas; “to be saved, to be accomplished” refers to the bodhisattvas not yet Buddhas; “not yet saved, not yet accomplished” refers to the heavenly dragons, ghosts, and spirits who have not yet ended birth and death.
[Kalpa] An abbreviation of the Sanskrit “kalpa.” It is an extremely long period of time, divided into small kalpas, middle kalpas, and great kalpas.
[Roots of good] That is, the good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; because these can give birth to the wondrous fruit, they are called the roots of good.
[Unobstructed wisdom] The wisdom that is free and unobstructed.

[Sravaka] One who hears the Buddha speak the Dharma of the four truths of suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path, and thereupon awakens. The sravakas have four stages of fruit, in order: srotapanna, sakrdagamin, anagamin, arhat.

[The Dharma of the four truths] Also named the four noble truths: the truth of suffering, the truth of accumulation, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path (abbreviated suffering, accumulation, cessation, path); “truth” means the true principle. The truth of suffering is the truth explaining that life is full of suffering; the “accumulation” of the truth of accumulation has the meaning of gathering together, and is the truth explaining how the suffering of life comes about; the truth of cessation is the truth that the realm of nirvāṇa alone is the final ending of suffering; and the truth of the path is the truth explaining how one must cultivate the path in order to realize nirvāṇa. These four noble truths exhaust the two-fold cause and effect of the world and beyond the world: accumulation is the cause and suffering is the effect, which is the cause and effect of the deluded world; the path is the cause and cessation is the effect, which is the cause and effect of the awakened world.
[Sravaka of the lesser fruit] The sravakas are those who cultivate the teachings of the lesser vehicle to realize the fruit, and so they are called sravakas of the lesser fruit.

[The three-thousand great-thousand world] That is, one great-thousand world; it is the region that a single Buddha teaches. One Mount Sumeru plus the four great continents is called a small world (according to the elder layman Huang Nianzu, a small world is one galaxy). Gathering a thousand small worlds is called a “small-thousand world”; gathering a thousand small-thousand worlds is called a “middle-thousand world”; and gathering a thousand middle-thousand worlds is called a “great-thousand world.” Because it three times counts the thousand, one great-thousand world is also called the “three-thousand great-thousand world.”

[The sands of the Ganges] The Ganges is one of the four great rivers of India; the Indians regard it as a sacred river, and its sand is fine and abundant. The Buddha often spoke the Dharma on both banks of the Ganges, and so he often uses “the number of the sands of the Ganges” to describe an exceedingly great number.

[The ten stages] From ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages in all: the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten dedications, ten stages, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. Among them the fifth group of ten is the ten stages (joyous stage, stage of separation from defilement, stage of radiance, stage of flaming wisdom, stage of extreme difficulty of victory, stage of the manifest, stage of the far-reaching, stage of the immovable, stage of good wisdom, stage of the Dharma cloud). In these ten stages one already belongs to the noble stage, and so they are also called “the ten noble ones.”

[Pratyekabuddha] One who, hearing the Buddha speak the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination, awakens; rendered into Chinese as “condition-enlightened” and “solitary enlightener.” “Pratyekabuddha” is a Sanskrit transliteration; the “buddha” here is only indicating the transliteration, the same as the sound “fo.”

[The twelve links of dependent origination] This explains the process by which conscious sentient beings revolve through birth and death. The twelve links are: ignorance (afflictions such as greed, anger, and delusion are the root of birth and death), action (the making of the various karma); consciousness (the karmic consciousness entering the womb), name-and-form (only the form of the embryo, not yet possessed of the six faculties), the six entries (the embryo grows into the human form with the six entries of eye and so on), contact (after birth, contact with external objects), feeling (contact with external objects gives rise to feelings of suffering and joy), craving (toward the objects there arises the desire of love), grasping (pursuing and creating), existence (the arising of good and evil karma); birth (again receiving the future five-skandha body), old age and death (the future body again gradually grows old and dies). These twelve items include all the cause and effect of illusion-raising, karma-making, and rebirth in the three times, turning round and round without end. (Among the twelve links, ignorance and action are the past life; consciousness, name-and-form, the six entries, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, and existence are the present life; birth and old age and death are the future life.)

[The lesser vehicle] “Vehicle” has the meaning of a conveyance, referring to the teaching by which one rides from the shore of delusion across to the shore of awakening. The dharmas of the sravakas and pratyekabuddhas take as their purpose self-cultivation and self-benefit; those saved are few, and their fruit is small, and so it is called the lesser vehicle; its highest fruit is the fruit of the arhat and the pratyekabuddha.

[The great vehicle] That is, the bodhisattva’s Dharma-gate, whose purpose is to save the world and benefit others; those saved are many, and its fruit is great, and so it is called the great vehicle; its highest fruit is Buddhahood.

[The heaven of the thirty-three] That is, Trayastrimsa. Because in the center of Trayastrimsa is the city of Shakra, the lord of the heavens, and in the four directions there are each eight heaven-cities, making thirty-three heaven-cities in all, Trayastrimsa is also called the heaven of the thirty-three.

[Elder] One who is eminent in virtue and learning, flourishing in wealth and resources, renowned far and near, a shelter for the orphaned and poor, and respected by the whole world, is called an “elder.”

[Seeing the Buddha’s auspicious marks, adorned with a thousand merits] The Buddha’s response body, from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, has thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks. Each hundred merits perfects one mark; the thirty-two marks require three thousand two hundred merits, called “the adornment of a thousand merits.”

[The three bodies] The Dharma body, the reward body, and the response body. The “Dharma body” is also named the self-nature body, or the Dharma-nature body; that is, the true nature that eternally abides, not arising and not ceasing, and is originally present in everyone — only that we sentient beings are deluded and do not manifest it, while the Buddha has awakened and realized it. The “reward body” is formed by the Buddha’s wisdom and merit, and has the distinction of the self-enjoyment reward body and the benefit-of-others reward body; the “self-enjoyment reward body” is the body by which the Buddha himself enjoys the inner-realized joy of the Dharma; the “benefit-of-others reward body” is the body manifested by the Buddha when he speaks the Dharma for the bodhisattvas of the ten stages. The “response body” is also named the response-transformation body, or the transformation body; that is, the Buddha’s body manifested in response to the conditions and opportunities of sentient beings.
[Nayuta] An Indian numeral, equivalent to the present “ten million” (one crore).
[Asamkhya] Rendered into Chinese as “innumerable”; that is, a number that cannot be counted out.

[The Dharma-image period] The Buddha-dharma’s destiny is divided into three periods: the right Dharma period, the Dharma-image period, and the Dharma-ending period. The thousand years after Śākyamuni Buddha’s nirvāṇa are the right Dharma period; though the Buddha has passed, the Dharma standards have not changed; there are teachings, there is practice, and there are those who realize the fruit, and so it is called the right Dharma period. The thousand years after that are the Dharma-image period; “image” means like; in this period there are teachings and there is practice, but those who realize the fruit are already few. In the ten thousand years after that is the Dharma-ending period; “ending” means slight; in this period it turns to what is slight and small, with only teachings and no practice, and those who realize the fruit are even rarer. We are now in the Dharma-ending period, and so the Great Collection Sutra says: “In the Dharma-ending period, though thousands of millions cultivate, rarely one attains the Way; only by reliance on Buddha-recitation can one pass beyond birth and death.”
[Brahmin] One of the four castes of India, rendered into Chinese as “pure practice”; it is the race that serves the great Brahma king and cultivates pure practices.

[The three jewels] The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are the three jewels. The Buddha is the discoverer of truth; the Dharma is the truth of the universe; the Sangha is the one who practices the truth. Because the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are all the most revered and most rare in the world and beyond the world, they are called the three jewels. Taking refuge in the three jewels is the first step of studying Buddhism. “In the vast sea of suffering there is nothing to rely on; only the three jewels are my refuge.” The three jewels are like a great Dharma-boat; seeing it and going to it is called “refuge” (gui); boarding the boat and sitting at ease, no longer sinking, is called “reliance” (yi).
[The noble maiden] This brahmin’s daughter had practiced for many lives and had deep merit from past lives, and so she is called a noble maiden.
[Evil destinies] That is, the evil paths.
[Tong] The same as “if,” “in case.”
[Min] The same as “to pity.”
[Bowing the head to the ground] The rite of laying the head on the ground, that is, “prostration”; this is a most supreme salutation. The character “qi” is pronounced “qǐ.”
[The iron encircling mountain] The iron mountain that encircles the salt sea and marks off a small world.
[Awe and spiritual power] Awe-inspiring virtue and spiritual power.
[The power of karma] The power of karma. Good karma has the power to produce the fruit of joy, and evil karma has the power to produce the fruit of suffering.

[If not by awe and spiritual power, then by the power of karma; without these two conditions, one ultimately cannot arrive.] The causes of reaching the hells are two: first, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas by their awe and spiritual power go to the hells to save beings; second, sentient beings who do evil, drawn by the power of karma, go to the hells to receive retribution. Without these two kinds of conditions, one could certainly never reach the hells.
[Jambudvipa] Also called the southern continent of Jambudvipa, rendered into Chinese as “the continent of surpassing gold”; that is, the Sahā world in which we dwell, also called southern Jambudvipa.

[Yojana] The unit name for measuring distances in India; there are the three distinctions of great, middle, and small. A small yojana equals forty Chinese li, a middle yojana sixty li, and a great yojana eighty li.
[The three karmas] Refers to the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
[What karma did he practice?] “Karma” refers to the actions created by body, speech, and mind.
[Returning to one's own place] Retreating back to the place one came from. “Que” means to retreat back.

[Not only the bodhisattva’s mother was freed from the hells; all the beings of the uninterrupted hell were, on that day, able to receive joy, all together reborn.] Relying on the merit of the brahmin’s daughter’s giving and offering, not only the brahmin’s daughter’s mother ascended to the heavens, but the benefit also reached the great host of the hells, and at the same time their offenses were reduced and all together they were born in the heavens.

[The brahmin’s daughter, as if waking from a dream, returned] The brahmin’s daughter soon, as from a dream, awoke. “Xun” means in an instant, soon. (The noble maiden, hearing the Buddha’s instruction, sat upright, reciting the Buddha for a whole day and night, entered the Buddha-recitation samādhi, in concentration reached the hells, and now, having achieved her aim, came forth from concentration.)

[Extensively setting up expedients, causing them to be liberated] Setting up all manner of skillful expedients to save the suffering, sinful sentient beings and cause them to leave the three evil paths.

blocks.text: Chapter Two: The Assemblies of the Transformed Bodies

inline.s: The Earth-Store Bodhisattvas of the transformed bodies from the hells of the ten directions, with the assembled sentient beings who had been liberated from the six paths, came to see the World-Honored One; the World-Honored One rubbed their heads and entrusted the Earth-Store Bodhisattva with a charge.

[Transformed bodies] Wherever there are the three evil paths, the Earth-Store Bodhisattva must divide his body and go to teach. Now the World-Honored One, at the palace of Trayastrimsa in Jambudvipa, was speaking the Dharma for his mother, and the Earth-Store Bodhisattvas of the transformed bodies of the ten directions all gathered at Trayastrimsa, participating in the Dharma-assembly, and heard the Buddha speak the Dharma.

[The karma paths] That is, the six paths of the round of birth and death. Karma is the good and evil done by body, speech, and mind. From these various karma as the cause, the fruit of birth and death is produced, and so they are called the karma paths.
[The round] Means that sentient beings, from beginningless time, turn in birth and death within the three realms and six paths, turning ceaselessly like a wheel.
[Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi] Rendered into Chinese as “the highest right and perfect enlightenment,” that is, the ultimate Buddha-fruit.
[The realization of the fruit] Here it is spoken as leaving the round of birth and death.

[Of every ten, one or two remain] The sentient beings of the Sahā world are obstinate and hard to teach; the Buddha, with his compassionate heart, saves them without abandoning them, causing their body and mind to be subdued, abandoning evil and turning to the right. Of ten parts, seven or eight have already been saved, and there is still one or two parts not saved, whose evil habits remain. The “ten parts” here refer to the sentient beings with whom Śākyamuni Buddha formed a Dharma-connection when he practiced the bodhisattva path in the past.
[The lord of the heavens] The lord of Trayastrimsa.
[The Brahma king] The great lord of the Brahma heaven of the realm of form.

[The wheel-turning king] Also called the wheel-turning sage-king, or the wheel-king; he is the most blessed person in the world, appearing when human life is eighty-four thousand years, and governing the four continents.

[Layman] Whoever possesses four virtues is called a layman: first, not seeking official rank; second, few desires and abundant virtue; third, dwelling in great wealth; fourth, guarding the Way and self-awakening. Here it does not mean one who studies Buddhism while living at home.
[Prime minister] A minister who assists in government.
[Officials and attendants] The civil and military officials and their staff.
[Upasaka] Rendered into Chinese as “pure faithful man.” That is, a man who, while living at home, draws near to and serves the three jewels and holds to the five precepts.
[Upasika] Rendered into Chinese as “pure faithful woman.” That is, a woman who, while living at home, draws near to and serves the three jewels and holds to the five precepts.
[Arhat] An abbreviation of arhat. “Arhat” is the highest fruit among the sravakas.
[Maitreya] The name of a bodhisattva who, after Śākyamuni Buddha, will descend into this world and become a Buddha in fifty-six hundred seventy million years.

[You should remember that I, at the palace of Trayastrimsa, earnestly entrusted this command: cause the sentient beings of the Sahā world, from now until Maitreya’s appearance, all to be liberated, to be forever free of all suffering, and to meet the Buddha and receive the prophecy.] Seeing sentient beings suffer, you should remember that I today at the palace of Trayastrimsa earnestly entrusted this command, causing the sentient beings of the Sahā world who suffer, from now until Maitreya’s appearance, all to attain liberation, to be forever free of all suffering, and to meet the Buddha and receive the prophecy. “Ling” here has the meaning of “to cause” and “to make.”

Yu fo (meeting the Buddha): First, meeting Maitreya Buddha; second, the thousand Buddhas of the auspicious aeon. All sentient beings from the Tathagata's parinirvāṇa until Maitreya attains Buddhahood are entrusted to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva, so that he guides the beings of the true, the semblance, and the final Dharma to study the Buddha's teaching, to be free of suffering and attain bliss, and in the future to receive the prediction of Buddhahood from Maitreya, and at the latest to gain liberation among the thousand Buddhas of the auspicious aeon.

Xian jie qian fo (the thousand Buddhas of the auspicious aeon): the aeon in which we now dwell is called the auspicious aeon, because within this aeon a thousand Buddhas come forth in succession. The first is Krakucchanda Buddha, the second Kanakamuni Buddha, the third Kasyapa Buddha, the present Śākyamuni Buddha is the fourth, and the future Maitreya Buddha is the fifth.
Shou ji (the prediction): to receive from the Buddha the assurance that one will certainly become a Buddha in the future.

Ti lei ai lian (tears of grief and longing): the sorrowful yearning and unwillingness to part has four meanings: first, grief that the beings of the six realms keep creating karma and will not change, refusing to cultivate the transcendental Dharma; second, grief that the beings are hard and obstinate, hard to transform, that the Dharma-boat is present before them yet they look upon it as if it were nothing; third, grief that the sun of the Tathagata's wisdom is about to set; fourth, grief that the great matter of the entrustment in the Trayastrimsa heaven is weighty.
Yi mao yi di (a hair and a drop): the same as a single hair and a single drop.
Shan zai! Shan zai! Wu zhu ru xi. (Well done! Well done! I rejoice for you.)
Excellent! Excellent! I rejoice for you, and I also aid your work of delivering beings and your early attainment of Buddhahood.

Pu ti (bodhi): translated into Chinese as 'awakening,' it refers to the wisdom that can know and awaken to the nature of dharmas, that is, the great wisdom that has completely cut off all afflictions.

blocks.text: Chapter Three: Contemplating the Karmic Conditions of Sentient Beings

inline.s: Queen Maya asked about the evil destinies brought on through the retribution of karma, and Ksitigarbha briefly answered concerning the five uninterrupted hells.
Guan zhongsheng yeyuan (contemplating the karmic conditions of sentient beings): using wisdom to observe the differences in the karmic causes created by sentient beings of the three realms.

Shi fajie (the ten Dharma realms): the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, the asuras, humans, gods, sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods) are the six ordinary beings; the last four (sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, Buddhas) are the four sages.
Yuan (conditions): refers to the interdependent relation of things, such as causes and conditions.
Sheng zhe (the sage): a transcendental sage who cuts off delusion and realizes the truth, benefiting self and others. Here it honors Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva of the stage of equal enlightenment.
Yan fu (Jambu): that is, Jambudvipa.
Qi shi yun he (how is this so): the circumstances of creating karma and receiving retribution, how is it, I do not know?
Cu shuo (to speak briefly): to speak in brief.
Wu jian diyu (the uninterrupted hell): a hell where one suffers without any interruption.

Bu xiao fumu, huo zhi shahai (to be unfilial to one's parents, or even to kill them): to be unfilial to one's parents, or even to kill them. Killing one's parents is one of the five deadly offenses, and one should fall into the uninterrupted hell, suffering for long aeons and seeking to escape with no end in sight. To be filial to one's parents and respect one's elders is the inherent culture of China and also the root of studying the Buddha's teaching.

Chu fo shen xue (to cause the Buddha's body to bleed): this is one of the five deadly offenses. The five deadly offenses are: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, causing the Buddha's body to bleed, and causing a schism in the samgha. The Buddha's response body cannot be harmed by ordinary beings; but if even a little blood is drawn, one commits the offense of causing the Buddha's body to bleed. If one deliberately damages an image of the Buddha, it is the same as causing the Buddha's body to bleed. ('Shi' means for one below to attack one above, causing injury or death. 'Shi' is read 'shi.')

He he seng (the harmonious samgha): when three or more bhiksus gather together, keeping the same precepts and practising the same path, they are called 'the harmonious samgha.' If someone uses means to make them separate, this is called 'causing a schism in the samgha,' and is one of the five deadly offenses.
Hui bang san bao (to slander the Three Jewels): deliberately vilifying the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Samgha.
Bu jing zun jing (to be disrespectful to the honored scriptures): to be disrespectful to the Buddhist scriptures.
Chang zhu (the permanent abode): refers to a Buddhist temple, where the Three Jewels dwell permanently and which is the place where sentient beings plant the field of blessings.
Dian (a flaw): a stain on white jade. 'Dian' is read 'dian.'
Qie lan (samgharama): an abbreviation of samgharama, translated into Chinese as 'the garden of the multitude,' that is, the garden where the monks dwell, and so the common name for a monastery.

Sha men (sramana): translated into Chinese as 'diligently pacifying,' meaning diligent in cultivating the Buddhist path and pacifying all afflictions; it is the common name for one who has left home to cultivate the Way.

Wei zuo sha men, xin fei sha men (to counterfeit a sramana, with a heart that is no sramana): outwardly displaying the appearance of a monk, with a shaven head and the monk's robe, while within one is no different from a worldly person, and by this means one damages and misappropriates the property of the monastery, which is the same as committing the five deadly offenses.

Po yong chang zhu (to break and use the permanent abode): wearing the black robe with a heart that has not left home, destroying and stealing the goods of the monastery, or appropriating the public good for private benefit and claiming it as one's own, is not the conduct of a monk.
Zi yi (the black robe): 'zi,' read 'zi,' black. The black robe is the black Dharma robe, and since ancient times the black robe has been used as a term for monks.
Qi kuang bai yi (to deceive the white-robed): to deceive and delude those who dwell at home. The white-robed refers to laypeople.
Zhong zhong zao e (creating all kinds of evil): the evil committed is not of a single kind; one creates various kinds of evil, even stopping at nothing.
Tou qie (stealing): to take things privately, without the consent of those in charge.

Why does stealing the goods of the monastery reach the offense of the uninterrupted hell? Because the goods of the monastery are donated by the benefactors of the ten directions to plant the field of blessings, offered to the Three Jewels of the ten directions, and belong to the Buddhas, the Dharma, and the Samgha of the ten directions. To steal the goods of the monastery is to commit an offense against the Three Jewels of the ten directions, and so the offense is grave. Within the gate of the Three Jewels, one may only make offerings and nurture blessings; unless permitted by the monks in charge, or openly given as a gift by the owner, one must never take things privately or damage them.
Za (to go around): the same as 'za,' to go round, to encircle.

Yu zhong you chuang, bian man wan li. Yi ren shou zui, zi jian qi shen bian wo man chuang; qian wan ren shou zui, yi ge zi jian shen man chuang shang. Zhong ye suo gan, huo bao ru shi. (In the hell there is a couch spreading over ten thousand li. One person undergoing punishment sees his own body lying over the whole couch; a thousand or ten thousand people undergoing punishment each likewise sees his own body filling the couch.) The ten-thousand-li couch of fire: whether one person or a thousand or ten thousand people, each sees his own body lying over the iron couch and suffering, because the evil karma they created has caused them to receive such a retribution.

Wan si qian sheng, ye gan ru shi. Dong jing yi jie, qiu chu wu qi. (A myriad deaths and a thousand rebirths; karma causes it thus. Passing through great aeons, seeking escape there is no end.) Dying at the extreme of punishment, and revived by the wind, dying and being born countless times, this is brought on by evil karma. Suffering for long aeons, it is difficult to gain release.

You wu shi ye gan, gu cheng wu jian. (Moreover, five matters of karma cause it, therefore it is called uninterrupted.) This clarifies the meaning of 'uninterrupted': again, because of the evil karma created, one receives the following five kinds of unbroken, endless retributions, and so it is called uninterrupted.

Yi zhe, ri ye shou zui, yi zhi jie shu, wu shi jian jue, gu cheng wu jian. (First, suffering day and night, through to the count of aeons, never interrupted, therefore it is called uninterrupted.) First, no interruption in time. Suffering continues day and night through countless aeons; to seek a single instant of rest, one cannot obtain it.

Er zhe, yi ren yi man, duo ren yi man, gu cheng wu jian. (Second, one person fills it, many people also fill it, therefore it is called uninterrupted.) Second, no interruption in body. Speaking in terms of no interruption in space, each sees his own body filling the couch and suffering.

San zhe, zui qi cha bang, ying she lang quan, dui mo ju zao, cuo zhuo huo tang, tie wang tie sheng, tie lu tie ma. Sheng ge luo shou, re tie jiao shen, ji tun tie wan, ke yin tie zhi. Cong nian jing jie, shu na you ta. Ku chu xiang lian, geng wu jian duan, gu cheng wu jian. (Third, the instruments of punishment: forks, clubs, eagles, snakes, wolves, dogs; pounding, grinding, sawing, drilling; chopping, hacking, boiling cauldrons; iron nets, iron ropes, iron donkeys, iron horses. Raw hide bound about the head, hot iron poured over the body, hungry one swallows iron pellets, thirsty one drinks iron broth. From year to year through the aeons, counted in nayutas. The torments of suffering are linked together, with never a break, therefore it is called uninterrupted.) Third, no interruption of the instruments of suffering. The fork stabs and the club strikes; the eagle devours and the dog bites; pounded to powder, ground to a pulp; the saw cuts the limbs, the drill picks out the flesh; the knife slashes and the axe cuts; the boiling cauldron and the oil pot; the net and the rope bind and entangle; the donkey and the horse trample; the living skin is flayed; the iron broth is poured over; iron pellets are food; iron broth is the soup. The skin is burned and the flesh broken, the bones charred and the marrow boiling, with pain after pain unceasing, through hundreds of millions of great aeons (counted in nayutas), with no end in sight.

Si zhe, bu wen nan zi nv ren, qiang hu yi di, lao you gui jian, huo long huo shen, huo tian huo gui, zui hang ye gan, xi tong shou zhi, gu cheng wu jian. (Fourth, without distinction of man or woman, of peoples foreign or barbarian, old or young, noble or base, whether dragon or spirit, god or ghost, all by the karmic power of their offense equally receive it, therefore it is called uninterrupted.) Fourth, no interruption in the object of the retribution. Whatever being commits the five deadly offenses and the ten evil acts equally receives the suffering of the uninterrupted hell. 'Qiang, hu, yi, di' is meant to include all races.

Wu zhe, ruo zhui ci yu, cong chu ru shi, zhi bai qian jie, yi ri yi ye, wan si wan sheng, qiu yi nian jian zan zhu bu de. Chu fei ye jin, fang de shou sheng. Yi ci lian mian, gu cheng wu jian. (Fifth, if one falls into this hell, from the first moment of entry through hundreds of thousands of aeons, in a single day and night one dies ten thousand times and is born ten thousand times, and to seek the briefest rest of a single thought one cannot obtain it. Unless the karma is exhausted, only then does one receive rebirth. Because of this continuous linking, it is called uninterrupted.) Fifth, no interruption in lifespan. From entering until leaving, each moment one dies ten thousand times and is born ten thousand times, never for an instant pausing, unless the karma is exhausted. Therefore the ancients explained hell as: 'unable to gain life, unable to gain death.'

blocks.text: Chapter Four: The Karmic Retribution of the Sentient Beings of Jambudvipa

inline.s: The Bodhisattva Samadhisvara again asked about Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva's past causes, and the Buddha briefly spoke of two matters. The four heavenly kings asked about Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva's great vow to deliver beings, and the Buddha related the Dharma of retribution that Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva had spoken.
Ye gan (karmic retribution): the creating of karma and the receiving of retribution. 'Karmic retribution' includes the cause, the condition, and the fruit, not one of which can be lacking.

Wo jin you meng fu fuzhu, zhi A yituo cheng fo yi lai, liu dao zhongsheng, qian ling du tuo. (I have now again received the Buddha's entrustment: until Ajita attains Buddhahood, I am sent to deliver the beings of the six realms.) 'Ajita' is the name of the Bodhisattva Maitreya; Maitreya is the family name, translated into Chinese as 'the Kindly One.' 'I' is Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva speaking of himself. I have now again received the Buddha's entrustment: all beings who form karmic ties in the period of the true, the semblance, and the final Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, when Maitreya Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood and delivers beings in the three assemblies, will all gain deliverance.

San hui (the three assemblies): when the Bodhisattva Maitreya in the future attains Buddhahood beneath the dragon-flower tree, in the first assembly he speaks the Dharma and delivers 9.6 billion beings; in the second assembly he speaks the Dharma and delivers 9.4 billion beings; in the third assembly he speaks the Dharma and delivers 9.2 billion beings.

Xing shi wu ding (the nature and consciousness are without stability): the nature and consciousness of sentient beings have no stable, fixed quality; lacking the wisdom to choose between good and evil karma, they are turned by circumstances.

E xi jie ye, shan xi jie guo (evil habits form karma, good habits form results): through the saturation of evil habits one creates evil karma and receives evil retribution; through the saturation of good habits one creates good karma and attains good results.
Wei shan wei e, zhu jing er sheng (doing good or doing evil, arising in response to circumstances): pursuing external conditions and circumstances, and so doing good or committing evil.

Lun zhuan wu dao, zan wu xiu xi (revolving through the five paths, never for a moment resting): revolving is a metaphor for birth in the six realms turning like a wheel; when good, one is born among the gods or as a human; when evil, one falls into the hells, the hungry ghosts, or the animals.

Wu dao (the five paths): first, the path of the hells; second, the path of the hungry ghosts; third, the path of the animals; fourth, the path of humans; fifth, the path of gods. Here the asuras of the six realms are, according to their differing levels, assigned respectively to the gods, humans, animals, and hungry ghosts.

Dong jing chen jie (moving through aeons of dust): the deluded mind creates karma, and often passes through aeons of dust without gaining release. This explains the great length of time of the wheel of transmigration. 'Dong' here means: at every turn, often.

Chen jie (aeons of dust): to grind the three thousand great thousand worlds into fine dust, and to count each grain of dust as one great aeon, this is the measure of time; it is a metaphor for a time extremely long.

Mi huo zhang nan (delusion, confusion, obstruction, and difficulty): this explains the causes of the wheel of transmigration. Deluded in the deluded mind, one gives rise to confusion, creates karma, and suffers; confusion, karma, and suffering unceasing; the three obstructions (the obstruction of afflictions, the obstruction of karma, the obstruction of retribution) are not dissolved. 'Difficulty' includes the eight difficulties, and for many aeons one wanders without meeting the Buddha's Dharma and without giving rise to faith, all because of the obstruction of the eight difficulties.

San zhang (the three obstructions): the obstruction of afflictions, the obstruction of karma, and the obstruction of retribution. 'Obstruction' means obstructing the holy path. The obstruction of afflictions, such as the confusion of greed, hatred, and ignorance; the obstruction of karma, such as the karma of the five deadly offenses and the ten evil acts; the obstruction of retribution, such as the painful retributions of the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals.

Ba nan (the eight difficulties): eight places and circumstances in which one is hindered from seeing and hearing the Buddha's Dharma, namely: the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, the northern continent of Uttarakuru, the heaven of no-thought, the blind, the deaf, and the dumb, worldly cleverness and eloquent intelligence, and the time before the Buddha's appearance and after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa. Among these, the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals belong to the three evil destinies, and because their karmic obstruction is too great, it is very difficult for them to see and hear the Buddha's Dharma; the people of the northern continent of Uttarakuru have great blessings, but they do not know the Buddha's Dharma, and so they cannot end birth-and-death; the heaven of no-thought is the place where non-Buddhists are born, and the people there too cannot end birth-and-death; those afflicted with blindness, deafness, or dumbness naturally cannot see or hear the Buddha's Dharma; worldly cleverness and eloquent intelligence refers to people who rely on their small cleverness and are unwilling to cultivate humbly, even going so far as to slander the Buddha's Dharma; those born before the Buddha's appearance or after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa cannot see the Buddha or hear the Buddha speak the Dharma.

Ru yu you wang, jiang shi chang liu, tuo ru zan chu, you fu zao wang. (Like a fish swimming in a net, taking it for the long river; released for a moment, then caught in the net again.) A metaphor for the wheel of birth-and-death: like a fish swimming in a net, mistaking it for the great river, now and then getting free of the net, and soon caught in it again. The reason beings wander through the three realms is entirely because of the net of the afflictions and karmic obstructions.

Ru ji bi shi wang yuan, lei jie chong shi, guang du zui bei, wu fu he lv. (Since you have fulfilled your former vows, with repeated great vows through many aeons, broadly delivering the guilty multitude, why should I now have any care?) 'Lei jie chong shi' (repeated great vows through many aeons): the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha, from beginningless aeons, has repeatedly renewed the great vow, 'Only when the beings are all delivered will I attain bodhi.' The 'chong' in 'repeated great vows' has two meanings: first, repeated, again and again, time after time; second, a 'zhong' (weighty) vow, a grave and great vow. The Dharma-burden has one to inherit it, and the Buddha, comforted, says: Since you, Ksitigarbha, are determined to complete the grave and great vows renewed through many aeons, and to deliver all beings who suffer through karma, why should I have any cause for care?
Ru lai (Thus-come-one): the Buddha has ten honorable epithets, namely:
First, Tathagata (Thus-come-one), coming to perfect enlightenment by the Way of suchness.
Second, Arhat (worthy of offerings), worthy of the offerings of gods and humans.
Third, Samyaksambuddha (the rightly and universally enlightened), truly and universally knowing all dharmas.

Fourth, Vidyacarana-sampanna (perfect in knowledge and conduct), possessing entirely the three knowledges (the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of heavenly vision, the knowledge of the extinction of outflows) and the five practices (the sage practice, the pure practice, the heavenly practice, the child practice, and the sick practice). ('The sage practice' refers to the bodhisattva practising the three karmas of precepts, samādhi, and wisdom; 'the pure practice' is the bodhisattva using a pure mind to apply compassion and remove suffering and give joy to beings; 'the heavenly practice' is the bodhisattva practising the wonderful practice according to the principle of natural true reality; 'the child practice' — the child is a metaphor for humans, gods, and the lesser vehicle, and the bodhisattva, with a compassionate mind, manifests the practices of humans, gods, and the lesser vehicle, which is called the child practice; 'the sick practice' is the bodhisattva, to deliver beings, with great compassion sharing the afflictions and sickness of all beings.)
Fifth, Sugata (well-gone), freely and well going forth into nirvāṇa.
Sixth, Lokavid (knower of the world), able to understand the principles and affairs of all worlds.
Seventh, Anuttara (the unsurpassed one), the unsurpassed supreme one.
Eighth, Purusa-damya-sarathi (tamer of men), able to tame and guide great men who cultivate the right path.
Ninth, Sasta-devamanusyanam (teacher of gods and humans), the Buddha is the teacher of all gods and humans.
Tenth, Buddha-bhagavat (the Buddha, the Blessed One), the Buddha is one revered by all the beings of the world.

Tong xing shi shan, rao yi zhongsheng (practising the ten good deeds together, benefiting sentient beings): governing the country with the ten good dharmas (not killing, not stealing, not committing adultery, not lying, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking idly, not coveting, not being angry, not being ignorant), so that the people's lives are rich and peaceful.

Qi lin guo nei, suo you renmin, duo zao zhong e, er wang yi ji, guang she fangbian. (Within the neighboring countries, all the people commit many kinds of evil; the two kings consulted and planned, and widely set up expedient means.) 'Neighboring countries' refers to the countries surrounding these two kingdoms. Because the two kings, having practised the ten good deeds, had people with few evils, while the neighboring countries were not within their jurisdiction and could not be taught, only then did they meet to discuss and plan.
Wei ru ding guan (entering samādhi to contemplate): the arhat, moved by the filial heart of the girl Bright-Eyes, entered samādhi to contemplate the place where her mother had been reborn.
Zi (to be self-indulgent): to let go, without restraint. 'Zi' is read 'zi.'

Ru ke zhi cheng nian qing jing lianhua mu rulai, jian su hua xingxiang, cun wang huo bao. (You may single-mindedly and sincerely recite the Tathagata Pure Lotus-Eye, and also sculpt and paint his image, and both the living and the dead will obtain retribution.) This shows the method of liberation. One is urged to recite the Buddha's name with a sincere mind, and to sculpt and paint the Buddha's image and make offerings. Dedicating this merit, both the living and the dead gain the supreme retribution.

Xu mi shan (Mount Sumeru): translated into Chinese as 'the wonderful high mountain.' This mountain is formed of four treasures — gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal — and so is called wonderful. No mountain can compare with it, so it is called high.

Cai jue ji han, ji dang yan shuo (only as soon as it felt hunger and cold, then it spoke): only as soon as it knew hunger and cold would it speak. Before completing three days, it could already speak and knew the affairs of its previous life; relying on the Buddha's power this was so, to awaken the mind of the girl Bright-Eyes; otherwise, having created hell-karma, how could it have such great spiritual power.

Lei duo da diyu (repeatedly falling into the great hells): the beings in the hells, in a single day, die ten thousand times and are born ten thousand times, and feel they are 'repeatedly falling into the great hells.'
Geng ye bei ti (sobbing and weeping sorrowfully): weeping until the voice is choked and breath caught, speaking with difficulty.
Zu (exhausted): finished; the suffering cannot be fully told. 'Zu' is read 'zu.'

San tu (the three destinies): the path of fire (the hells); the path of blood (the hungry ghosts), eating raw flesh and drinking blood, eating unclean food; the path of knives (the animals), suffering the torment of the knife and the slaughter.
Ju wen (fully heard): to hear completely.
Fan zhi (brahmin): Sanskrit, meaning 'the pure clan.' Here it refers to a renounced brahmin.
Yi fu (garments): here it refers to banners, canopies, streamers, and other cloth ornaments.

Su ming (past lives): the lives of previous existences. The Buddha said that people in past lives all had lives, whether as gods, humans, hungry ghosts, or animals, revolving in transmigration; one who can know past lives is said to have the knowledge of past lives (the divine eye of recollection of former abodes).

Yin man bu duan (the karmic vine unbroken): since beginningless time, the evil habits of sentient beings have not ceased, the wheel of transmigration has not stopped, and they do not seek liberation; confusion, karma, and suffering are born again and again, like a vine climbing and entangling, intertwining and binding.

Su yang (former misfortunes): many disasters life after life. 'Su' originally means past. In the past one killed many living beings, and in this life one meets with disasters; here 'su' includes the present life, and if one does not change in this life, the next life will bring even worse misfortune. Killing beings shortens their lives, and so one receives the retribution of short life and much illness.

Qie dao (stealing and robbery): 'qie' means privately, secretly. To take what is not given is stealing; to seize it forcibly as one's own is robbery; robbery is the extreme of stealing. The retribution of the thief is lack of food and clothing, and all affairs going contrary to one's wishes, with all kinds of retributions of poverty, distress, and suffering.

Xie yin (sexual misconduct): for one who dwells at home, apart from the rightful spouse, to commit impure conduct between men and women. Those addicted to lust, following their habits, fall into the animal path and become lustful birds.
E kou (harsh speech): to wound others with coarse and evil words, receiving the retribution of discord and endless disputes among one's six kinds of relatives, life after life.

Hui bang (slander): to maliciously ruin another's reputation, charging the most groundless accusations, is called 'slander.' A 'tongueless' is a mute. Or one falls into the animal path, and though having a tongue, it does not function. 'Sores in the mouth' means the mouth rots and breaks out in sores.

Chen hui (anger and hatred): this belongs to the mental karma. Greed, anger, and ignorance are the fundamental afflictions of sentient beings. When angry, the brows are knit and the eyes glare, both eyes fiercely bulging, the face hideous, the face red and the ears hot, so the flower retribution and the remaining retribution bring about ugliness, lameness, and deformity, and the direct retribution falls in the hells. 'Long' is read 'long,' a hunchback. 'Disability' is mutilation, the faculties incomplete.

Hua bao, yu bao (the flower retribution and the remaining retribution): a flower blooms before the fruit, so the 'flower retribution' is the retribution that comes before the 'direct retribution.' The so-called flower retribution is creating karma in the present life and receiving the retribution in the present life. The so-called direct retribution is creating karma in the present life and receiving the retribution in the next life; the direct retribution is far greater than the flower retribution. The 'remaining retribution' is the leftover retribution received in the life following the direct retribution, for example, after leaving the hells, receiving the body of an animal.

Qian lin (stinginess): 'qian lin' means to have yet not to give. The miser, who would not pluck a single hair from his body for the benefit of all under heaven, receives the retribution that whatever he seeks, nothing turns out to his satisfaction.
Yin shi wu du (immoderate eating and drinking): eating and drinking without restraint, indulging and squandering at will.

Tian lie zi qing (hunting at will): 'tian' is in ancient times the same as 'tian.' 'Tian lie' means hunting, which belongs to killing life. Giving free rein to hunting and killing wild creatures, causing them to be startled and to lose their lives, so too one receives the retribution of losing one's mind and losing one's life.
Bei ni (disobedience and rebellion): 'bei' means to go against, to be disobedient. If one is unfilial to one's parents, one receives the retribution of being killed in natural calamities.

Shao shan lin mu (to set fire to mountain forests): setting fires on the mountain, the deep groves hold many tiny lives, and so many lives are harmed; once the thick smoke rises, the beings are frightened and lose their minds, and so one feels the retribution of madness, losing one's way, or falling into a fire-pit, drowning in water, or falling into a valley and losing one's life. Therefore farmers or foresters must never burn weeds.

Qian hou fumu (former and later parents): 'former and later parents' means stepfather and stepmother. 'Fan sheng' means in return. If one is a stepfather or stepmother and abuses and beats the children of a former or later union, in turn one will also receive the retribution of being beaten.

Wang bu sheng chu (to net and catch young birds): 'chu' is a young bird. Catching young birds, causing them to be torn from their own flesh and blood, so too one receives the retribution of separation from one's six kinds of relatives.
Hui bang san bao (slandering the Three Jewels): blindness, deafness, and dumbness are the remaining retribution, and the direct retribution is in the hells.

Qing fa man jiao (to slight the Dharma and despise the teaching): if one slights the right Dharma, or even profanes it, destroying the wisdom-eye of sentient beings, one abides forever in the evil destinies and rarely meets the sage's teaching.

Po yong chang zhu (to break and use the permanent abode): if one maliciously damages or misappropriates the goods of the monastery, appropriating the public for the private, for aeons one dwells constantly in the hells and suffers.
Wu fan wu seng (to defile the pure practices and slander the monks): if one defiles another's pure practice and slanders the treasure of the Samgha, one falls forever into the animal path.

Tang huo zhan zhuo (boiling water, fire, beheading, and hacking): this belongs to killing karma. If one uses boiling water, scorching fire, the knife, and the axe and other means to wound and kill beings, one feels the wheel of mutual devouring, a retribution of one requital for one, not the least bit off. The saying goes: 'Eat half a catty, give back eight taels,' not a hair's difference. 'Zhuo' is read 'zhuo.'

Po jie fan zhai (to break the precepts and violate the fast): 'zhai' means to take no food after noon, that is, not to eat after midday. Having made the vow to take the precepts and then breaking them, having made the vow not to eat at improper times and then not keeping it, in the future one falls into the animal path, becoming birds, beasts, and evil animals, and constantly suffering the retribution of hunger.

Fei li hui yong (to destroy and misuse things contrary to reason): not using things to the full, not sparing implements, such as a quarrelling couple smashing things to vent their anger, will surely bring the retribution of lack and want and ruin.

Wu wo gong gao (self-importance and arrogance): in being a person one must be humble, and only humility brings benefit; otherwise, with arrogance and conceit, not only does the Dharma-water not enter, but in the next life one is born a lowly person, at the beck and call of others.

Ruo yu liang she dou luan zhe, shuo wu she bai she bao (if one meets one who stirs up disputes with divisive speech, one speaks the retribution of a tongueless and a hundred-tongued): 'two tongues' is newly translated as 'divisive speech.' Stirring up discord; in the worst case it costs lives, in the least case it hurts feelings. One who uses the tongue to stir up trouble and sow division receives the retribution of being mute (no tongue) and of many mouths attached to one body (a hundred tongues).

Xie jian zhe (one of wrong views): wrong views means not believing in cause and effect, denying cause and effect, or taking what is not a cause as the cause and what is not an effect as the effect; the retribution is to be born in the border regions, where one does not meet the Buddha's Dharma.

blocks.text: Chapter Five: The Names of the Hells

inline.s: The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra asked about the names of the hells and the evil retributions, and Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva answered.

Pu xian pusa (the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra): one of the four great bodhisattvas of Buddhism (the four great bodhisattvas are Manjusri, Samantabhadra, Avalokiteshvara, and Ksitigarbha), renowned for great practice. The ten great vows of Samantabhadra: to worship all Buddhas, to praise the Tathagatas, to make the broadest offerings, to repent of karmic hindrances, to rejoice in the merit of others, to request the turning of the Dharma-wheel, to request the Buddha to abide in the world, to follow the Buddha's teaching always, to accord with sentient beings always, and to dedicate all merit universally.
Ren zhe (the benevolent one): one possessed of great compassion and great vows. This is the honorific with which bodhisattvas address one another.
Si zhong (the four assemblies): the two assemblies of renounced men and women and the two assemblies of laymen and laywomen.
Sui (profound): read 'sui,' meaning deep and distant.

A bi (avici): Sanskrit, translated into Chinese as 'uninterrupted,' that is, the uninterrupted hell. It is a hell where suffering is unbroken, the place where those who have committed the gravest offenses fall after death.

Si jiao diyu (the hell of the four corners): the walls are of hot iron, and raining down are fire and iron; the offender hides in the four corners of the wall, but in truth there is no place to hide or flee.
Fei dao diyu (the hell of flying knives): the knives are like wheels, descending in a whirl, hacking and cutting the offenders.
Huo jian diyu (the hell of fire arrows): iron arrows set aflame are shot into the offenders' bodies.
Jia shan diyu (the hell of pressing mountains): two mountains press together, crushing the offenders into a pulp of flesh.
Tong qiang diyu (the hell of the piercing spear): the spear, an ancient weapon, a kind of knife or lance. The spear entering the chest and coming out the back is called 'piercing the spear.'
Tie che diyu (the hell of iron chariots): hot iron chariots run over and crush the offenders.
Tie chuang diyu (the hell of iron couches): lying upon iron couches, suffering the torment of scorching and roasting.
Tie niu diyu (the hell of iron oxen): being trampled by iron oxen.
Tie yi diyu (the hell of iron garments): using red-hot iron as garments, causing the body to be scorched and burned.
Qian ren diyu (the hell of a thousand blades): the hell of knives and mountains, butchering and cutting the offenders.
Tie lv diyu (the hell of iron donkeys): making one ride an iron donkey, the body and mind scorched and aflame.
Yang tong diyu (the hell of molten copper): the offender drinks melted copper broth, and the five viscera are all reduced to pulp.
Bao zhu diyu (the hell of embracing the pillars): the offender embraces red-hot copper pillars.
Liu huo diyu (the hell of flowing fire): fire like a river, burning the offenders.
Geng she diyu (the hell of plowing the tongue): the jailer pulls out the tongue and plows it with an iron ox and a hot plow.
Cuo shou diyu (the hell of beheading): a chopping knife cuts off the offender's head.
Shao jiao diyu (the hell of burning feet): the feet tread on hot iron, swelling, painful, and festering to a pulp, like the goose-web that worldly people love to eat.
Dan yan diyu (the hell of devouring eyes): the eyes of the offender are devoured.
Tie wan diyu (the hell of iron pellets): iron pellets are the food, and when hungry one swallows iron pellets.
Zheng lun diyu (the hell of disputes): entering the hell of disputes, one quarrels and curses without cease.
Tie fu diyu (the hell of iron axes): a cleaving knife hacks and cuts the offender. 'Fu' is a cleaving knife used to cut grass; in ancient times it was also used as an instrument of execution.
Duo chen diyu (the hell of much anger): those given to greed, resentment, and hatred enter the hell of much anger; dying in anger and reviving, in this way again and again.
Jiao huan diyu (the hell of crying out): the offender shrieks in torment and wails.
Ba she diyu (the hell of the pulling of the tongue): the same as the earlier hell of plowing the tongue.
Fen niao diyu (the hell of excrement and urine): that is, the hell of boiling excrement and urine.
Tong suo diyu (the hell of copper chains): copper chains bind the offender's body.
Huo xiang diyu (the hell of fire elephants): making the offender ride a fire elephant.
Huo gou diyu (the hell of fire dogs): making the offender ride a fire dog.
Huo ma diyu (the hell of fire horses): making the offender ride a fire horse.
Huo niu diyu (the hell of fire oxen): making the offender ride a fire ox.
Huo shan diyu (the hell of fire mountains): the whole mountain is gathered fire.
Huo shi diyu (the hell of fire stones): fire stones are the seat.
Huo chuang diyu (the hell of fire couches): the same as the earlier hell of iron couches.
Huo liang diyu (the hell of fire beams): the beams are all of fire, making one hang from them or embrace them.
Huo ying diyu (the hell of fire hawks): fire hawks peck at the flesh.
Ju ya diyu (the hell of saw-teeth): an iron saw saws the teeth.
Bobang diyu (the hell of flaying): as for a person who slaughters cattle and snakes.
Yinxue diyu (the hell of drinking blood): the blood of the offender is drunk.
Shaoshou diyu (the hell of burning hands): the offender's hands are burned.
Shaojiao diyu (the hell of burning feet): the offender's feet are burned.
Daoci diyu (the hell of reversed barbs): iron barbs pierce upward into the offender, hooking his flesh backward.
Huowu diyu (the hell of the fire house): the house is made of hot iron, its flames blazing.
Tiewu diyu (the hell of the iron house): its name differs slightly from the fire house, but the meaning is the same.
Huolang diyu (the hell of fire wolves): fire wolves devour the offenders.
Yegan rushi (such is the retribution of karma): the painful retributions of the hells described above are all the fruits that sentient beings of Jambudvipa encounter by doing great evil karma.
Neng di Xumi (able to rival Mount Sumeru): the power of karma is so great that it outweighs Mount Sumeru.
Neng shen juhai (able to deepen the great ocean): the power of karma is deeper and broader than the sea.
Neng zhang shengdao (able to obstruct the holy path): such is the great power of karma that it blocks the practice of the transcendental holy path, so one cannot perfectly fulfil one's learning.
Xianhao shou zhi (even a hair's breadth must be received): however small the evil, like a hair, one must still receive its retribution.
Yecha shi zhi (the yaksha eats it): the yaksha (a man-eating ghost) eats the offender's heart.
Huotang sheng fei (the cauldron of soup boils fiercely): the hell of the oil cauldron boils the offender's body. 'Sheng' means fierce, raging.
Chen ji zuiren (rushing upon the offender): 'chen' means to chase, to pursue.
Yixiang hanbing (unbroken icy cold): the hell of ice and cold.

Chun fei jili (flying caltrops): 'jili' were weapons made of iron like spiked balls, used in ancient warfare. This hell is filled with red-hot iron spiked balls that fly back and forth, striking and piercing the offenders.

Wufei shi tong, shi tie, shi shi, shi huo (it is none other than copper, iron, stone, and fire): because when sentient beings do evil, their anger is like fire and their minds like iron and stone, utterly cruel with not a trace of softness, so their instruments of punishment likewise are none other than copper, iron, stone, and fire.
The Buddha emitted light and a great voice praising the Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha. The Bodhisattva Puguang asked about the benefits, and the Buddha explained them at length.
Fei ren (non-humans): refers to the ghosts and spirits among the eight classes of devas and nagas that resemble humans but are not human.
Miedu (extinction): that is, nirvāṇa, also called entering extinction.
Dingshou (receive upon the head): expresses the utmost reverence, bearing the teaching upon the crown of one's head.
Diting (listen attentively): to listen with careful attention.
Weiran (so be it): to assent respectfully: yes.
Zengcai (colored silk): 'zeng' (read zeng), a general term for silk textiles; zengcai means colored silk, used to make offerings to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas and to adorn the place of practice.
Chuangfan (banners and streamers): flags used to adorn the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and the place of practice; the cylindrical ones are chuang (banners), and the long streamers are fan.
Shiqing zhi jian (within the time of a meal): the time it takes to eat a single meal.

Zuo zhu jiyue (making various kinds of music): playing various kinds of sublime music that brings forth joy and a pure mind in people, such as Sanskrit hymns and Dharma music, nurturing the thought of the Way and guiding people to give rise to faith, and with beautiful melodies praising the supreme virtue of the great being; not ordinary worldly music. 'Ji' (read ji) generally refers to song and dance performance.

He kuang qin shou zhu heng (how much less to suffer calamities in person): that is, one does not meet with sudden calamities and disasters. Those who cultivate the Dharma-gate of Ksitigarbha can obtain the protection of hundreds and thousands of ghosts and spirits, so that whether in this life or the next they can dissolve calamities and avert misfortune.

Wang sheng ji hui (rashly generating ridicule and slander): recklessly spreading rumors, mocking and defaming, denying the benefits of the cultivators' merit, and destroying others' aspiration for the Way.
Huo lu chi xiao (or baring the teeth in laughter): or laughing wildly without restraint.

Xian jie (the auspicious aeon): the present great aeon. Because in this aeon a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, it is called the auspicious aeon, also called the good aeon. Our teacher Śākyamuni Buddha is the fourth Buddha among the thousand Buddhas of the auspicious aeon.
Egui (hungry ghosts): these ghosts have throats as thin as needles, bellies as large as drums, and flames of hunger issuing from their mouths.

Zhu gen bu ju (imperfect faculties): 'the faculties' refers to the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. 'Imperfect faculties' refers to being crippled, idiotic, insane, and the like.
Jiu chu chuang zhen (long abiding on bed and pillow): to be long bedridden with illness.

Huo you xian dao, huo duo yanmei, gong guishen you (or wandering in dangerous paths, or often haunted in slumber, roaming with ghosts and spirits): often having nightmares, or dreaming of evil ghosts at night, or dreaming of deceased relatives and friends, or dreaming of wandering in evil realms, or dreaming of walking mountain paths fraught with danger, or being pressed down by a night-mare ghost and unable to move, or dreaming of roaming together with ghosts and spirits. 'Yan' is read 'an.'
Wangzhai (wasting illness): 'wang' (read wang) means extremely weak; 'zhai' (read zhai) means internal and external injury, often referring to consumption.

Yedao lundui (debate and confrontation in the karmic paths): these all arise from the accumulated evil karma of past lives, and at the time of death, in the realm of karma or before King Yama, one's enemies and creditors argue and confront one.
Wei ding qingzhong (not yet determined light or heavy): the offense has not yet been judged.
